name: InSight
keyDiscovery: Recorded 1,319+ marsquakes, mapped Mars's crustal thickness (24–72 km), confirmed a large liquid metallic core with radius of 1,830 km, and detected seismic waves from fresh meteorite impact craters.
missionLegacy: Operated for over four Earth years (1,445 sols) until December 2022, providing humanity with our first comprehensive 3D internal structural map of another rocky planet.
funFact: On May 4, 2022 (Sol 1222), InSight recorded a monster magnitude 4.7 marsquake that shook the entire planet, causing seismic waves to reverberate across the crust for more than ten hours.
heritageNote: InSight rests permanently in the flat volcanic plain of Elysium Planitia, its circular UltraFlex solar panels blanketed in thick orange regolith dust.

objects.name: InSight Hexagonal Lander
objects.description: A high-stability hexagonal deck constructed of aluminum honeycomb with carbon composite face sheets, supported by three landing legs. It carried UHF and X-band communications, avionics, and the RISE geodetic rotation antennas.
objects.scienceDiscovery: RISE radio science antennas tracked the wobble of Mars's rotational axis to sub-centimetre precision, proving that the planet's core is liquid and molten.
objects.legacy: Operated quietly for over 1,445 sols, enduring severe regional dust storms before transmitting its final farewell signal in December 2022.
objects.firstPerson: I touched down in the smooth red sand of Elysium Planitia. My job was not to roam, but to listen. For four Earth years, I sat motionless under the two moons, letting the deep vibrations of Mars tell me the ancient story of its birth.

objects.name: SEIS Ultra-Sensitive Seismometer
objects.description: France's CNES Seismic Experiment for Interior Structure consists of three very-broad-band sensors sealed in an evacuated spherical vacuum chamber, sheltered under a thermal and aerodynamic Wind and Thermal Shield (WTS) dome placed directly on the soil.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Discovered that Mars is seismically active, recording 1,319+ marsquakes, and mapped the thickness of the Martian crust and the depth of the liquid core boundary.
objects.legacy: The most sensitive planetary seismometer ever built, capable of detecting vibrations smaller than the width of a single hydrogen atom.
objects.firstPerson: Beneath my golden dome, sealed in a silent vacuum, I felt the ground pulse. I heard deep tectonic rumbles in Cerberus Fossae and felt space rocks smash into the red plains thousands of kilometers away. I felt the heartbeat of Mars.

objects.name: HP³ Heat Flow Probe ('The Mole')
objects.description: Germany's DLR Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package featured a 40-centimetre self-hammering tungsten penetrator designed to burrow 5 metres underground, trailing an instrumented cable with 14 temperature sensors to measure geothermal heat escape.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Discovered that the Martian regolith in Elysium has unexpected cohesive properties, forming a cement-like duricrust that challenged hammering mechanisms.
objects.legacy: After months of innovative robotic teamwork with the IDA scoop pushing the mole, the instrument fully characterized the thermal conductivity of the upper 40 cm of soil.
objects.firstPerson: I was 'The Mole', built to burrow deeper into another planet than any machine before me. The Martian duricrust was tough as rock, but with my team gently pressing my back with the robotic scoop, I buried myself into the soil and measured the warmth of the planet's interior.

objects.name: Twin UltraFlex Solar Arrays
objects.description: Two 2.15-metre diameter circular fan-fold arrays with ultra-lightweight carbon composite ribs and triple-junction solar cells. They generated 4,600 watt-hours per sol at landing, tapering to 300 watt-hours as dust accumulated.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Demonstrated the durability of UltraFlex circular array designs and provided empirical data on wind-driven dust accumulation rates across multi-year missions.
objects.legacy: The gradual coating of red dust led to poignant final communications that captivated millions around the globe in December 2022.
objects.firstPerson: I opened like twin golden wheels against the pink sky. For four years I caught the morning light, but no cleaning dust devil ever swept my wings. As the red powder thickened, my power faded, but I gave every last drop of current until my lights went out.

objects.name: Instrument Deployment Arm & Camera
objects.description: A 1.9-metre robotic arm with 4 degrees of freedom, an instrument grapple claw, a scoop, and the Instrument Deployment Camera (IDC). It was used to autonomously pick up SEIS, the WTS dome, and HP³ and place them millimeter-accurately onto the regolith.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Successfully demonstrated precision placement of delicate science experiments onto an unprepared planetary surface for the first time in space exploration history.
objects.legacy: Pioneered soil-trickling operations, dropping sand grains onto the solar arrays to allow wind to scour away clinging dust particles.
objects.firstPerson: I was the arm that unpacked our science. With my claw, I gently picked up the seismometer, lowered it to the red dirt, and covered it with its aerodynamic shield like a sleeping child under a blanket. In my final months, I scooped sand over our solar cells to help the wind blow them clean.

objects.name: TWINS Weather & Pressure Sensors
objects.description: Spain's CAB Temperature and Wind Sensors for InSight boom, paired with an ultra-high-resolution atmospheric pressure sensor capable of detecting barometric drops as small as 0.1 Pascal as dust devils passed over the lander.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Tracked thousands of passing vortex dust devils, correlating micro-barometric dips with the acoustic and seismic signals picked up by SEIS.
objects.legacy: Provided continuous daily weather bulletins that revealed daily boundary layer convective turbulence patterns in the Martian tropics.
objects.firstPerson: Every sol at noon, I felt invisible whirlwinds race across the plains of Elysium. As dust devils whipped past my mast, my pressure sensors dipped in fractions of a second. I showed that Mars breathes with turbulent, dancing energy.
